t: Why Being An Authoritarian Teacher Is A Big Mistake
q: Kids don’t misbehave because they don’t want discipline. They misbehave because they do.
If the discipline is meted out by an authoritarian, it will be met with private resentment and rebellion—especially among your most difficult students.
Rules are a form of executive order. They come down via royal decree and are not to be questioned. Just followed without complaint.
Everything you do, from rules and consequences to policies and routines, must have a compelling reason why you’re doing it .
Every classroom management policy must have a why that students understand. And you must be ready to explain it to them. “Because I said so” doesn’t cut it.
They’re for them and wholly and completely for their benefit.

t: Why You Need To Stay The Course With Difficult Students
q: Difficult students are treated like temperamental orchids, forever subject to trial and error. What works for awhile never seems to last, so let’s try something else.
It’s to stay the course. It’s to be the same steady, calm, and kind teacher who follows the same progression of consequences day after day and week after week.
You see, with your most challenging students, improvement doesn’t happen overnight. It takes time. A slow turn of an oil tanker.
You do what is best for them long term by relying on the natural law that we learn when lessons come from realizing our own mistakes.
You must believe in them and have the toughness to say no to degrading tokens, prize boxes, rewards, and fake praise.
Treat your toughest students with the same dignity and good humor as your very best.

t: How to Heal a Divided World: Argumentative Writing that Actually Listens to the Other Side ative-writing-that-actually-listens-to-the-other-side
q: In many places, students are taught a standard model to present their own points and "shoot down" elements of their opposition. While this feels triumphant, especially with a one-reader teacher-audience, it doesn't equip students to communicate in healthy and productive ways.

With a team of teacher researchers -- Dave included -- I spent time the last few years examining the pitfalls of argumentative writing and crafted methods to teach students to use nuance and empathy to achieve productive civil discourse.
Aside from writing that has great potential to solve the political divide of our world (no small feat, right?), essays that practice empathy are more dynamic and interesting to read.

Students need to pivot from just grabbing a quote from each article -- if you've taught research writing for more than a day, you know this is standard practice -- to actually understanding how the message, the audience, and the communicator are perceived by supporters and opponents of their topic.
He wanted to shift his claim from "The government should make abortions illegal" to a more nuanced "The government should support pregnant mothers.

When teaching this step, I physically pulled two chairs together in the front of my classroom and talked to the imaginary person on the other side of my issue. I picked up their invisible, emotional knapsack and held it in my arms, bearing the heaviness of their heart.
We have an opportunity when we teach argumentative writing to turn the opposition back into an actual person. We can teach students to sit right next to their adversary on middle ground.
Not only will this make the writing more mature and dynamic, but -- with empathy and nuance -- our young writers might actually change someone's mind and help heal this divided world.

t: How To Handle Students With ODD

It must be an every-time enforcement of rules, even and especially if the student behaves egregiously in response. In fact, any defiant reaction must also be enforced.
It’s the authoritative nature of how they’re held accountable that students with ODD rail most against, not the accountability itself.

If a student with ODD likes you because you provide trust and stability by doing what you say you’re going to do, and by being consistently kind, then you’re 90 percent of the way there in helping them take responsibility rather than blaming you or pointing the finger elsewhere.
They begin to overcome the ODD label they’re saddled with and build empathy and understanding brick by brick.
